chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about the Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the owner's death), is he from the one-third [of the estate]? He said, 'Yes, and the testator has the right to return [revoke or modify] in his will, whether he bequeathed in health or in sickness.'

key_terms.أَوْ مَرَضٍ: Or sickness: The state of the testator, indicating the right to revoke persists even during illness.
key_terms.اَلثُّلُث: The third: The portion of the estate that can be bequeathed to non-heirs.
key_terms.اَلْمُدَبَّر: Mudabbir: A slave whose manumission is contingent upon the death of the master.
key_terms.فِي صِحَّةٍ: In health: The state of the testator when making the initial bequest.
key_terms.لِلْمُوصِي: For the testator: The person making the will/bequest.
key_terms.يَرْجِعَ: To return/revoke: The right to alter or cancel the bequest.

ai.seo_question: Is a Mudabbir included in the one-third share of the estate for bequests in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the Mudabbir, a slave designated for manumission upon the owner's death, is counted within the one-third share of the estate bequeathable to non-heirs, a ruling derived from the principle that such bequests do not exceed the disposable third. The Imam further establishes the testator's absolute right to modify or revoke this specific bequest at any time, whether during health or illness, highlighting the flexibility of testamentary disposition in Shia jurisprudence. This ruling underscores the distinction between the Mudabbir's status as a bequested entity versus a fixed heir, allowing for dynamic estate management.
